The economic benefits of tax cuts depend significantly on the type of tax cut, who it targets, and the time horizon considered. Research shows that corporate income tax cuts generate "large and persistent" positive effects on the economy in the long run, while personal income tax cuts tend to have effects concentrated in the short run [d1]. Broad-based cuts like the Tax Cuts and Jobs Act (TCJA) were associated with investment growth (4.5% above pre-TCJA projections in 2018), job creation of 3.2 million new jobs, and unemployment reaching near 50-year lows [d4][d5][d9], and were credited with reducing tax burdens on farmers and small businesses [d2][d12]. However, tax cuts specifically targeting the rich show little to no significant effect on overall economic growth or unemployment, though they do increase top income inequality [d3][d8], and cutting corporate tax rates is not reliably associated with gains in median wages for typical workers [d6]. The IMF finds that while tax cuts provide a one-time boost to GDP, consumption, and investment, "these effects are never strong enough to prevent a loss of revenue," meaning cuts must be financed through debt, spending reductions, or other taxes [d7]. Stimulus-oriented tax cuts during recessions, such as those in the Recovery Act, provided immediate economic relief to over 95 million households [d13], while pro-growth tax policy more broadly aims to reduce distortions to labor supply, saving, and investment [d11][d12].
